questions.question: Explain the difference between innate and adaptive immunity. / [CO5] [2x5 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the difference between innate and adaptive immunity. [U] [CO5]
  • Innate immunity is the body's immediate, non-specific defence against pathogens, while
  • adaptive immunity is a more specialized and long-lasting response that develops after
  • exposure to a specific pathogen. Innate Immunity does not target a specific type of pathogen
  • but responds to a broad range of invaders. It is present at birth providing a rapid response. It
  • includes skin, mucous membranes and phagocytes
  • Adaptive Immunity recognizes and targets specific pathogens. It develops over time as the
  • body is exposed to pathogens or vaccines. It involves B cells (which produce antibodies)
  • and T cells (which directly attack infected cells).

questions.question: What is central dogma of molecular biology? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is central dogma of molecular biology? [K]/[CO3]
  • The components of the Central Dogma
  • The process consists of three main stages
  • A. Replication: DNA acts as a template to produce more DNA, ensuring genetic
  • information is passed on.
  • B. Transcription
  • The process where a specific segment of DNA (gene) is copied into a single-
  • stranded RNA molecule (mRNA).
  • C. Translation: The mRNA molecule is read by ribosomes in the cytoplasm,
  • translating the RNA sequence into a specific sequence of amino acids to form a
  • protein.

questions.question: Name the major organs of the digestive system and their functions. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Name the organs of digestive system and their functions. [K] [CO2]
  • The organs of digestive system and their functions are the following: -
  • • Mouth: Initiates digestion by mechanical breakdown (chewing) and chemical
  • digestion (saliva).
  • • Pharynx: A passageway for food and air.
  • • Oesophagus: Transports food from the pharynx to the stomach by peristalsis.
  • • Stomach: Stores food, mixes it with gastric juices (acids and enzymes), and begins the
  • breakdown of proteins.
  • • Small Intestine: Completes digestion and absorbs most nutrients.
  • • Large Intestine: Absorbs water and electrolytes, forms faeces, and stores waste before
  • elimination.
  • • Rectum: Stores faeces.
  • • Anus: Eliminates waste from the body.
  • Accessory Organs:
  • • Salivary Glands: Produce saliva, which contains amylase that breakdown
  • carbohydrates.
  • • Liver: Produces bile, which aids in the digestion of fats.
  • • Gallbladder: Stores and concentrates bile.
  • • Pancreas: Produces enzymes that digest carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, as well as
  • hormones that regulate blood sugar.

questions.question: What is the circulatory system, and why is it important? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What is circulatory system? Why is it important? [K] [CO2]
  • The circulatory system is a vital network responsible for transporting blood throughout the
  • body. It is composed of the heart, blood and blood vessels that include arteries, veins,
  • capillaries.
  • Importance of circulatory system:
  • • Oxygen and Nutrient Delivery: The circulatory system carries oxygen from the lungs and
  • nutrients from the digestive system to all parts of the body. This is crucial for cellular
  • function and energy production.
  • • Waste Removal: The circulatory system transports waste products, like carbon dioxide,
  • from cells to the lungs for exhalation and other organs for elimination.
  • • Hormone Transport: The circulatory system also carries hormones, which are chemical
  • messengers that regulate various bodily functions.
  • • Immune Function: The circulatory system helps transport immune cells to fight off
  • infections and diseases.
  • • Temperature Regulation: The circulatory system plays a role in regulating body
  • temperature by distributing heat to different parts of the body.
